Structure-loss paper · urban conflagrations

Trees, fences and wind in urban conflagrations · 2026-10-13

Our 2002–26 record (726 fires), the USGS Carlson record 2002–22 (361) and CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25 (445) · pre-fire tree canopy between neighbouring buildings (two years before each fire), a tree-linked version of the building block, hourly wind gusts, public fence data, and the big losses in sparse treed housing (Gatlinburg, Black Forest, Bastrop)

By Carlo Broderick, NCEAS, UC Santa Barbara · started 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT · updated 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT

We asked whether trees, fences or wind explain the fires the building rule gets wrong. The rule: a fire that reaches a block of more than 89 closely spaced buildings can become an urban conflagration (≥ 50 destroyed buildings joined within 30 m); of the 24 fires in our 2002–26 record that reached such a block, 10 did. Trees between the houses do not explain which of those became urban conflagrations, and linking houses through trees does not improve the rule. Wind was strong in most of them. Trees do matter in a different kind of loss: in forested towns like Gatlinburg, many scattered houses burned in a chain carried by the forest. Fences cannot be tested: no public map exists.PA36 (prereg commit 46db1c3). T1 not shown; T2 no better; leak flag on year − 1 → primary canopy year = ignition year − 2. Three records: Carlson 2002–22, our 2002–26 record, CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25.

How to read this page

Biggest block: the largest group of buildings standing before the fire whose centres are within 35 m of a neighbour in the group (about 20 m wall to wall). Urban conflagration: at least 50 destroyed buildings in one connected patch, each within 30 m (centre to centre) of another destroyed building in the patch. Gap canopy: pre-fire tree cover in the 30 m square between two neighbours. Hover any dot, cell or heading for details; switch to Technical for methods.

Update 2026-10-13: buildings outside the U.S. removed

The building set behind this page held some buildings across the border. They are now removed: every building must lie inside the United States (Census Bureau state boundaries). 13 fires lost buildings (Harris 2007, Border 3 2016, Border 32 2022, Caribou 2017, 9 Mile 2015, Eagle Bluff 2023, Granjeno 2023, Border 60 2024, Goosmus 2024, Los Ebanos 2024, Border 6 2025, Massey Way 2025, Sol 2025); 27,181 buildings in all, 380 of them among the buildings a fire reached; 19 had been called destroyed by our damage model alone (Granjeno 2023: 1, Border 6 2025: 18), none in Carlson's hand-mapped record or CAL FIRE's inspections.

What changed here: Harris 2007's biggest block was in Tecate, Mexico; with U.S. buildings only it holds 42 buildings (was 141), so it drops below the 89-building line. Fires above the line in our 2002–26 record: 25 → 24 (10 urban conflagrations in both). False alarms of the buildings-only rule: 15 → 14. Gap canopy, urban conflagrations vs not: 10.9% vs 12.0% (p 0.71) → 10.9% vs 12.0% (p 0.71). Peak gust: p 0.71 → 0.69. No conclusion on this page changed.

Added 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT

Trees between the houses of the biggest block

Of the 24 fires in our 2002–26 record that reached a block of more than 89 closely spaced buildings, 10 became urban conflagrations (at least 50 destroyed buildings in one connected patch). Tree canopy between the houses was not higher in those 10: median 10.9% vs 12.0% in the 14 that did not (p 0.71). The share of house-to-house links passing through trees was 7% vs 0% (p 0.49). The other two records agree. What it suggests: trees between houses do not explain which big blocks became urban conflagrations.T1 (prereg PA36): primary measures G1 (mean canopy at link midpoints) and G2_25 (share of links with midpoint canopy ≥ 25%), USFS Science TCC v2025-6 at ignition year − 2 (year − 1 failed the leak check). Exact or 200,000-draw permutation tests on the difference of medians, Holm over {G1, G2}; bar Holm p < 0.05 in R2 with the same sign in R1 and R3: not shown. Supporting Firth logit (R2, ≥ 100 exposed, n 355, 10 events): adding standardised G1 to log10(1 + block) gives LR p 0.23; leave-one-fire-out AUC 0.986 → 0.982 (Δ CI -0.011 to +0.001).

How this panel was checked
  • Like for like: every fire uses the same 30 m canopy map, read two years before its own ignition; the same 35 m link rule as the conflagration line.
  • Leakage: a canopy map made after a fire sees burned trees. Year − 1 failed the pre-registered leak check (the destroyed-minus-surviving canopy gap dropped by 0.18 points from year − 2 to year − 1, CI -0.26 to -0.11), so year − 2 is used; year − 1 gives the same answer (in the table file).
  • Small n: 10 vs 14 fires, so only large differences could be detected; exact permutation tests, intervals from resampling fires.
  • U.S. buildings only (since 2026-10-13): Harris 2007 is no longer above the line (biggest block 141 → 42 once 292 buildings in Mexico are removed), so 10 vs 14 fires, not 10 vs 15.
  • Claims: 'not shown', not 'no effect'; the intervals are wide.
Added 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT

Does a 'fuel-linked' block predict better?

Linking houses through trees (up to 60 m apart, with canopy all the way between) does not predict better than buildings alone. In our 2002–26 record (726 fires, 10 conflagrations) the ranking score went from 0.993 to 0.990, and the rule caught the same 10 conflagrations with 22 false alarms instead of 14. What it suggests: keep the building-only definition; trees mostly add forest towns that did not become an urban conflagration.T2: Firth logit on log10(1 + FLB_25_60) vs log10(1 + b20), leave-one-fire-out AUC and mean log score; paired fire bootstrap (2,000) of ΔAUC. Bar 'better' = higher log score in all three records and R2 ΔAUC CI above 0: no better. Sensitivities (canopy ≥ 50%, reach 80 m, year − 1, ≥ 100 exposed) are in docs/paper/tables/p30_t2_flb.csv; none passes the bar.

Three towns: buildings, links and pre-fire tree canopy

Three towns, one tab each: a block that became an urban conflagration (Tubbs, Coffey Park area), a large block that did not (Creek 2017, Sylmar), and a big loss in sparse, treed housing (Gatlinburg). In Coffey Park the houses are close enough to link without trees; in Gatlinburg the links exist only through the forest. Tubbs 2017, Santa Rosa: 637 buildings, 278 destroyed, 1,368 grey and 2 green links; Creek 2017, Sylmar: 453 buildings, 20 destroyed, 1,181 grey and 5 green links; Chimney Tops 2 2016, Gatlinburg: 516 buildings, 493 destroyed, 212 grey and 605 green links.Points: Carlson exposed buildings (direct, counted, known outcome) in the view box (biggest block, or for Gatlinburg the largest through-trees destroyed chain, + 150 m). Lines: pairs ≤ 35 m (grey) and 35–60 m passing the canopy rule (green). Raster: USFS Science TCC, ignition year − 2. Added 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT

Big losses in sparse, treed housing

Below the line (the 331 fires with ≥ 100 exposed buildings whose biggest block is ≤ 89), fires with more tree canopy around houses lost a larger share of them, but only weakly (rank correlation 0.25). Of the 37 big sparse losses (≥ 300 destroyed), 3 form a chain of 50+ destroyed buildings only when links through trees are allowed. Gatlinburg (Chimney Tops 2, 2016) is the clearest: 1,517 destroyed, never more than 16 within 30 m of each other, but 326 joined through continuous tree canopy. What it suggests: in forested towns, trees can carry fire between houses that are too far apart to ignite each other; that is a different kind of town loss from a dense urban conflagration.T3 (descriptive): Spearman of G3a (canopy within 30 m of exposed buildings) with destroyed share 0.25 [0.14, 0.35], with LDC50 0.20 [0.09, 0.30], n 331 (R2, b20 ≤ 89, ≥ 100 exposed). Fuel-linked destroyed chain FLDC = destroyed links ≤ 30 m or 30–60 m with every 10 m canopy sample ≥ 25%; the plain 60 m chain shows what reach alone gives (Erskine, Dixie: long chains, but not through trees). Outcome-side and descriptive; the definition itself is PA34's study.

Added 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT

Wind: most were wind events

Most of these fires were wind-driven. Published reports describe a strong offshore or downslope wind for 6 of the 10 that became urban conflagrations and 10 of the 14 that did not (the rest were not checked). Airport gusts in the first two days were similar: median 18.0 vs 15.9 m/s (p 0.69). What it suggests: wind is what lets a fire reach a town, but among fires that reached a big block in a wind event, wind does not tell which became urban conflagrations.Descriptive only (fire weather is not a model input). IEM ASOS/AWOS, 3 nearest stations ≤ 75 km with ≥ 12 reports, ignition date 00:00 local + 48 h. Primary (nearest station gust): 17.0 vs 15.7 m/s, p 0.61 (9 vs 12 fires with a gust report); shown: max of 3 stations. Daily gridMET wind/VPD were already null (PA31).

Added 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT

Sharper canopy maps (CHMv2, lidar) where they exist before the fire

The 30 m canopy map used above agrees with sharper canopy-height maps where both exist: rank correlation 0.86 with the 0.6 m CHMv2 model on pre-fire air photos (150 fires) and 0.70 with pre-fire lidar (68 fires). Only 6 of the 25 big-block fires have a CHMv2 map from before the fire; on those, the two that became urban conflagrations (Tubbs, Sandalwood) do not stand out. What it suggests: the coarse map ranks fires the same way as the sharp ones, and on the six big-block fires the sharp map covers it tells the same story.L2: de_space CHMv2 (DINOv3) on NAIP, chm_ge2mfracRing0_100ft, used only when NAIP year < ignition year: 150 of 244 Carlson fires (Camp, Woolsey, Glass, Marshall, Almeda Drive, Creek 2020 and Chimney Tops 2 used same-year NAIP and are excluded). L3: stage-67 3DEP lidar, lid_canfrac_ge2m_r30, acquisition year < ignition year by construction, fire mean over pool buildings. Spearman vs TCC G3a (year − 2).

Fences: no usable public data

There is no usable public map of fences. In 22 of the 27 town blocks checked, OpenStreetMap has no fence mapped at all, although a fenced lot would add tens of metres of fence per house. Where fences are mapped (Almeda Drive, Sayre, Marshall), OpenStreetMap shows today's rebuilt town, not the fences that stood before the fire; What it suggests: fences cannot be tested with public data; the literature (below) treats them as a real house-to-house path from field studies and experiments.OSM via Overpass (ODbL), box = biggest exposed block + 50 m; median fence length per OSM building 0.0 m (prereg rule: < 10 m → no usable data). OSM is a present-day snapshot, so even complete fence mapping would be post-fire. County parcel data do not record fences.

Added 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT

What others found about trees, fences and wind between houses

Field studies agree with what we see: the spacing of buildings comes first; vegetation near a house matters for that house and inside a burning town, but adds little to explain which towns become urban conflagrations. Fences and other small fuels are a known path from house to house in experiments and NIST case studies, but no study maps them at the scale needed here. No peer-reviewed Lahaina study with a DOI was found that measures trees or fences between buildings.Every DOI resolved on Crossref on 2026-10-13; claims come from the abstracts (reports without abstracts are cited for their scope only).
